title: Flexible Pipes and Flexible Risers
analyses: Global static and dynamic response analysis
Tensile armour stress and fatigue analysis
Minimum bend radius and overbending analysis
Flexible pipe fatigue and service-life assessment

models.text: The suite should implement Cauchy elasticity, generalized Hooke's law, axial and circumferential stress formulations, Lamé thick-cylinder theory, nonlinear beam and rod models, Cosserat rod theory, torsional elasticity, shell buckling, geometric nonlinear finite-element formulations and pressure-induced deformation models.

The suite should include helical armour wire equilibrium, multilayer axisymmetric analysis, pressure armour deformation models, interlayer contact stiffness, frictional slip models, helical wire bending and torsion, coupled axial–bending–torsional stiffness, composite cross-sectional models and anisotropic equivalent stiffness formulations.

The suite should implement internal pressure burst criteria, external pressure collapse models, nonlinear shell instability, carcass collapse models, wet-collapse models, pressure-induced ovalization, radial instability and imperfection-sensitive collapse analysis.

The suite should include Brazier ovalization, nonlinear curvature relationships, interlayer slip–stick models, armour wire buckling, radial instability, birdcaging mechanisms, local wrinkling, minimum bend-radius models and nonlinear contact instability.

Applicable methods include nonlinear catenary theory, Morison's equation, added-mass and drag models, vessel-motion response, effective tension calculations, fluid–structure coupling, seabed contact and touchdown-zone nonlinear dynamics.

The suite should incorporate transient heat conduction, thermal expansion, temperature-dependent material behaviour, pressure-dependent stiffness, annulus pressure modelling, internal pressure cycling and coupled thermomechanical finite-element analysis.

The suite should include S–N fatigue curves, rainflow counting, Palmgren–Miner damage, multiaxial fatigue criteria, critical-plane fatigue methods, fretting fatigue, interlayer wear, armour-wire fatigue and progressive material damage.

The suite should combine global nonlinear riser models with detailed three-dimensional multilayer finite-element calculations, analytical helical-armour formulations with nonlinear contact, CFD-informed hydrodynamic loading with time-domain dynamics, and fatigue damage calculations with inspection-based condition assessment. Multiscale global–local modelling is especially important because global riser response does not directly resolve every individual armour wire, interlayer contact stress or local carcass deformation.

Elastic and plastic stress-strain curves, tensile strength, yield strength, stiffness, density, thermal expansion and fatigue characteristics.
Fluid density, temperature, pressure, composition, phase conditions and flow rates.
Water depth, seawater density, external hydrostatic pressure and annulus pressure.
Internal operating pressure, hydrotest pressure, pressure cycling, emergency depressurization and pressure differentials.
Axial tension, curvature, torsion, imposed displacements, vessel motions and installation loading.
Friction coefficients, contact stiffness, gap dimensions, wear properties and interlayer slip characteristics.
Armour-wire strength, fatigue properties, wire spacing, number of wires and pre-existing damage.
Termination geometry, connector stiffness, mechanical load rating, seal characteristics and armour anchorage geometry.
Wave and current conditions, drag coefficients, added mass and vessel-induced motions.
Lay tension, chute radius, reel diameter, bending cycles, deployment sequence and handling equipment limits.
Annulus flooding condition, corrosive fluid exposure, hydrogen sulfide content, carbon dioxide content and material ageing properties.
Allowable pressure, curvature, strain, tension, fatigue damage, layer utilization and design life.

subtitle: Multilayer flexible pipes, pressure armour, tensile armour, carcass collapse, birdcaging, bending and end-fitting integrity.
ic: The initial conditions shall define the flexible pipe or riser centreline configuration and its multilayer cross-sectional construction. This includes the carcass, pressure sheath, pressure armour, tensile armour, anti-wear layers, insulation and outer sheath.

The initial structural state shall establish axial tension, curvature, twist, interlayer contact pressures, initial gaps and pre-existing manufacturing or installation stresses. The pipe may initially be considered straight and unloaded for a manufacturing-level analysis, or in its installed equilibrium configuration for in-service analysis.

Pressure simulations shall initialize internal fluid pressure, external hydrostatic pressure, annulus pressure and relevant layer contact conditions. Wet-collapse assessments shall distinguish initially dry annulus conditions from cases with an already flooded annulus.

Thermal analysis shall initialize the temperature of the fluid, metallic layers, polymer layers and surrounding environment. Fatigue simulations shall include the initial accumulated cyclic damage and any known armour-wire deterioration.
For installation simulations, the initial state shall include pipe reel curvature, deployment tension, overboarding configuration and suspended length as appropriate.
bc: Global mechanical boundaries shall prescribe appropriate end constraints, imposed vessel motions, pipeline-end connections, top tension and bending or rotational conditions.

At the layer interfaces, contact boundaries shall permit physically appropriate interlayer friction, separation, sliding and compression while preventing unrealistic penetration. Carcass and pressure-armour interactions shall represent their actual structural contact behaviour.

Internal pressure shall be applied to the appropriate pressure-containing surface or layer, while external hydrostatic pressure shall act on the external boundary. Annulus pressure conditions shall be prescribed according to the annulus sealing, venting or flooding state.

Thermal boundaries shall represent internal fluid heat transfer, conduction through individual layers and heat transfer to external seawater. End-fitting boundaries shall transfer axial loads, bending moments, torsion and pressure reactions through the actual termination structure.

For minimum bend radius analysis, prescribed bending or contact geometry shall create the required curvature. Installation boundaries shall apply reel or chute contact, lay tension, vessel motion and seabed touchdown conditions.

calibration: Calibration should use full-scale flexible pipe qualification testing, manufacturer-certified material data, pressure tests, collapse tests, cyclic bending tests, torsion tests and tensile fatigue experiments.
Layer-specific material stiffness and plasticity should be calibrated using material coupon experiments and representative component tests.
Pressure armour and tensile armour interaction should be calibrated using instrumented axial loading, bending and torsion tests.
Interlayer friction and slip behaviour should be calibrated using controlled tests involving realistic layer contact pressures, temperature and cyclic deformation.
Carcass collapse, wet-collapse and external pressure instability models should be informed by representative hydrostatic chamber tests and measured failure pressures.
Birdcaging and radial instability parameters should be calibrated using controlled tensile loading and pressure-release experiments.
End-fitting load transfer should be calibrated using full-scale termination tensile, bending, pressure and fatigue testing.
Thermal response should be calibrated using temperature-dependent material tests and thermal cycling experiments.
For flexible risers, global hydrodynamic response and damping should be calibrated using submerged dynamic tests and instrumented operational measurements.
Fatigue models should be calibrated using armour-wire fatigue tests and representative full-scale flexible pipe fatigue programmes.
verification: Global flexible pipe response should be verified against suspended-line and beam benchmarks with appropriate effective stiffness properties.
Multilayer cross-sectional finite-element models should undergo mesh convergence, contact convergence and material implementation testing.
Axial tension, bending, torsional response and pressure containment should be checked using independently calculated reference cases.
Interlayer contact and friction should be verified using controlled contact problems involving sticking, sliding and separation.
External pressure collapse models should undergo numerical imperfection sensitivity testing, load-step refinement and instability benchmark comparisons.
Carcass collapse and birdcaging predictions should be checked for appropriate nonlinear solution convergence and sensitivity to geometric imperfections.
End-fitting calculations should undergo local mesh refinement, contact verification and equilibrium checks.
Fatigue calculations should be tested using reference stress histories and independent damage calculations.
Thermal–mechanical coupling should be checked using known thermal expansion and temperature-dependent material benchmarks.
validation: Predicted axial stiffness, bending stiffness and torsional response should be compared against independent full-scale flexible pipe mechanical testing.
Layer stresses and deformations should be evaluated using instrumented cross-sectional specimens and full-scale tests where internal measurements are available.
Pressure containment and burst resistance should be validated using qualified pressure-to-failure experiments.
External collapse and wet-collapse predictions should be assessed against independent hydrostatic test results.
Birdcaging and armour instability should be validated using representative failure experiments.
Interlayer slip, friction and hysteresis should be assessed using cyclic mechanical tests.
End-fitting reaction and fatigue predictions should be compared against independent termination qualification tests.
Installation and global dynamic response should be assessed using recorded deployment conditions and available operating measurements.
Fatigue and remaining-life predictions should be compared with representative full-scale fatigue tests, material tests and service inspection records.
Validation should explicitly distinguish unbonded flexible pipes from bonded flexible pipes and should not assume that test results transfer between materially different layer constructions.

geometry.text: Unbonded flexible pipes, flexible risers, metallic carcasses, polymeric pressure sheaths, pressure armour, tensile armour, anti-wear layers, outer sheaths, bend stiffeners, bend restrictors and end fittings.

geometry.cat: Conventional and universal CAD geometry formats
geometry.text: STEP, IGES, Parasolid, ACIS, DXF and supported DWG should be accepted for flexible pipe assemblies, helical metallic layers, polymeric layers, connectors, interlocking carcasses, end fittings and ancillary components.

STEP and Parasolid solids, IGES surfaces, DXF cross-sectional profiles, SVG vector profiles and documented CSV, XML or JSON cross-sectional descriptions should be supported. The importer should reconstruct individual layers, wire cross-sections, helical winding directions, helical pitch, layer thickness, contact interfaces and cross-sectional eccentricities where needed.

CSV, XYZ, JSON, XML, DXF three-dimensional polylines, GML and GeoJSON with suitable three-dimensional coordinates should be accepted for catenary configurations, lazy-wave profiles, seabed routes, dynamic touchdown positions and connection geometry.

Abaqus INP, Nastran BDF, ANSYS CDB, Gmsh MSH, MED, UNV, VTK/VTU and Exodus should be accepted for compatible global beam representations, localized multilayer solid meshes, interlayer contact models and detailed end-fitting analysis.

STL, OBJ, PLY, GLB, LAS/LAZ, E57, GeoTIFF and XYZ point clouds should be supported for damaged flexible pipes, deformed carcasses, complex bend restrictors, scanned end fittings and irregular touchdown-zone geometry.
